The 4 levels of using AI at work How to use AI at work: there are four levels, and most people never leave level one. Chat. You paste something into ChatGPT or Claude, it answers, you copy it back out. Useful, but you're the delivery guy carrying every answer between your apps by hand. Context. Give it your price list, your process docs and ten emails you wrote so it learns how you sound. Same AI, completely different answers, because now it answers like it works at your company. Connected tools. Out of the box, AI can't open your CRM or read your spreadsheet. Almost every app has a door for other software called an API, and MCP is a standard plug that lets AI walk through those doors. Once it's connected, it sees your contacts, your sheets and your email, and it acts: update, send, create. Updating 2,000 customer records from last month's invoices is two weeks of somebody's life. Connected AI does it in minutes. Run it on ten records first, check them, then let it do the rest. Automations. Level three still needs you to ask. Level four starts on its own: a new lead comes in, an invoice lands, Monday at 8am. A tool like n8n moves the data between your apps, and the AI in the middle does the thinking: reads the email, picks the category, writes the reply. Your business keeps running while you sleep. The whole ladder: chat, context, connected tools, automations. On level three you talk and it does the work. On level four you don't even have to talk. If you want to climb all four, from your first chat to your first AI automation, I built seven courses for exactly that, in order, inside my community. I made a video breaking down AI agent observability and evals, and ran the whole thing on open source. If you build agents, sooner or later you watch one run and realise you have no idea what it just did, or what it cost you. That gap is what observability and evals are for. Least glamorous part of the stack, and the part you end up needing most. Observability is a camera. It records what ran, how long, what it cost. Eval is a referee. It decides whether the run was good enough to ship. I ran it on @treg_ai for the tool calls and @waku_agent for the memory. treg is an OpenRouter for agent tool calls, so your agent carries one API key instead of one per tool. Both open source, so you can read the code rather than take my word for it. You Can Build Anything. You Can Learn Anything. 💪
